← Gutter install bid calculator

How much to charge to install gutters

The number a homeowner wants is a published “$4.50 a foot installed” gutter special, or a price they saw for a ranch hang on a coupon site. That number is not a takeoff. A 140-foot one-story 5-inch aluminum hang with two included downspouts is not the same job as a 220-foot two-story 6-inch hang with extra drops, inside miters, forty feet of fascia, and tear-off of the old system. The trip is the same. The hours are not.

Open the free bid calculator

Count the corners and the drops, not just the feet

Gutter-cleaning calculators price stories and downspouts for a wash. Gutter-guard calculators price mesh on an existing trough. A new hang is a different job: the trough, the miters, the drops past the included first two, the stories, and the fascia that is not in the coupon. Quoting all of that from a published per-foot special is how the first inside miter eats the field margin.

A job with the same trip can cost much more

Each extra drop past the included first two is time that never appears on the coupon. A second story is billed as its own hours. Inside miters, fascia, tear-off, and hidden hangers are adders that get forgotten on a brochure special. On the sample rates a 220-foot 6-inch aluminum colonial with two inside miters, four downspouts, 40 feet of fascia, tear-off, and hidden hangers prices about $6,782.18 ($30.83 per foot of gutter, 32.3 crew-hours). The same shop’s 140-foot 5-inch ranch prices about $1,749.03 ($12.49 per foot, 8.1 hours, walk-away $1,189.34). Matching the brochure job’s $4.50 special on the two-story house is how that job becomes a loss — the walk-away on the heavy job is already $4,611.88, and the $4.50 special ($630 on the ranch) loses $559.34 even on the brochure hang.

Copper and tear-off are not automatically a markup on the ranch

A 160-foot two-story copper hang with steep access and tear-off is not the 140-foot ranch plus 15%. On the sample rates that copper job prices about $7,396.97 ($46.23 per foot, 21.6 crew-hours) — more than the brochure hang, not because copper is slower to hang but because story hours, steep access, and an $18-per-foot trough do not live in a published ranch special. An 180-foot one-story 5-inch hang with tear-off and a third downspout prices about $2,851.79 (14.0 hours). Treating either as a blended add-on is how the special that looked fine turns into a loss after the first inside miter.

Load the wage, then keep a walk-away number

A $38/h installer loaded at 32% payroll burden is $50.16. Margin is a share of the price you send, not a markup on cost. The walk-away price is total cost — below that the job makes nothing before you take a dollar home. Replace every rate with your invoices before you send either number.

What this is not

This is not a gutter design, a water-management plan, a building-code determination, a permit, an engineering stamp, or a recommended market price. It is arithmetic on the numbers you type. Footage, profile, stories, miters, downspouts, fascia, and tear-off are yours to confirm. It does not price a cleaning route or a gutter-guard install.

Price your gutter hang

Common questions

How much to charge to install gutters?

Charge from the trip, the hang, inside and outside miters, extra downspouts past the included first two, extra downspout footage past ten feet per drop, second-story hours, fascia, tear-off, loaded labor, overhead, and a margin that is a share of price. A default 140-foot one-story 5-inch aluminum ranch with four outside miters and two included downspouts, at the sample rates in this calculator, prices around $1,749 — about $12.49 per foot of gutter.

Why is a $4.50-a-foot gutter special dangerous?

Homeowners count linear feet. Corners, extra drops, extra downspout footage, a second story, fascia rot, and tear-off do not scale with that number. Matching a cheaper special written for a one-story ranch is how a two-story colonial with fascia becomes a two-day loss. On the sample rates the $4.50 special is $630 on the ranch and already $559 under the walk-away cost.

How much to charge to install gutters on a two-story house with fascia?

A two-story six-inch hang with extra drops and fascia is not a ranch-only special. On the sample rates a 220-foot 6-inch aluminum colonial with two inside miters, four downspouts, 40 feet of fascia, tear-off, and hidden hangers prices around $6,782 ($30.83 per foot, 32.3 crew-hours), while a 140-foot 5-inch ranch prices around $1,749 ($12.49 per foot, 8.1 hours).

No warranty. This page and the calculator are free and as-is. They are not construction, legal, tax, financial, or engineering advice. You are responsible for verifying every figure before you rely on it or send a bid.

Bid the corners, the drops, and the stories.

Price a new gutter hang the way the trade actually loses money: inside and outside miters, extra downspouts past the included first two, extra downspout footage past ten feet per drop, second-story hours, fascia repair, and tear-off. You get the bid, the price per foot of gutter, and the walk-away number below which the job loses money.

The house

Where the hours go

    Where the cost goes

      Transparent arithmetic from your own inputs. Starting hours and material rates are common ballpark figures, not an industry standard or a water-management design — replace them with your own takeoff.

      Hand the customer a proposal

      The price above is for you. This is the page you print or save as a PDF and give to the customer — your details, their details, the scope, the deposit split, and a line for them to sign. Your business details are saved on this device so you only type them once; the customer’s details are never saved.

      Everything on the printed page is text you typed or a number this calculator worked out. It contains no warranty, lien, or cancellation wording — those depend on your jurisdiction and your contract, and this tool is not the place to invent them.

      Common questions

      Why does the calculator only charge for downspouts past the first two?

      Because a per-foot special is usually built around a brochure job that already includes a couple of drops and ten feet of downspout each — so those defaults are subtracted out before anything is billed. Extra downspouts and extra downspout footage past that included allowance are the only ones that add their own labor and material lines, which is why two houses with the same gutter footage but different drop counts can price very differently.

      Why does a two-story house cost more per foot of gutter than a one-story of the same length?

      Story hours scale with gutter footage, not with a flat add-on — one story adds nothing, two stories add 0.018 hours per gutter foot, and three stories add 0.032, on top of steep-access hours if that's checked too. A 220-foot run on a two-story colonial carries real ladder and staging time that the same 220 feet on a one-story ranch never needs.

      Why does copper cost so much more than aluminum for the same run?

      Mostly material, not labor: half-round copper starts at $18 per foot of trough versus $3.40 for 5-inch aluminum, while the hang labor only runs modestly higher at 0.055 hours per foot versus 0.035. Six-inch aluminum sits in between on labor (0.04 hours per foot) but adds its own $1.20-per-foot profile premium on top of the base aluminum rate, which a straight per-foot comparison to 5-inch aluminum would miss entirely.

      Why are inside miters priced differently from outside miters?

      They're two separate line items with their own hours and their own material cost per corner, because an inside corner and an outside corner are cut and sealed differently — the calculator doesn't assume a fixed inside-to-outside ratio the way a flat per-foot special implicitly does. A run with mostly outside corners and one with the same corner count split evenly between inside and outside can price differently.

      Does tear-off of the old gutters only add a dump fee?

      No — it's a toggle that adds its own labor hours (per foot of gutter) as well as its own dump-fee material line, and both scale with the length of the run being torn off, not a flat charge regardless of size. Left unchecked, tear-off contributes nothing to either the hours total or the material total, which is the difference between a fresh-fascia install and a strip-and-replace.

vs-a-flat-per-foot-special.html.text:
← Gutter Install Bid Calculator

This calculator vs. a flat $4.50-a-foot special

Names no specific product or company. This compares a free calculator against the generic pricing habit gutter shops are shopped against every day: one flat per-foot rate — commonly a "$4.50 a foot installed" special — advertised the same regardless of stories, corners, downspouts past the included allowance, fascia condition, or tear-off.

First — the flat special is right, and you should have one

A yard sign or a web estimate needs a number before anyone has walked the house. "$4.50 a foot installed" is a perfectly fine headline rate, and no calculator replaces having one. What follows is not an argument that the flat rate is wrong. It is what that same rate stops showing you the moment a house is real and you know its footage, profile, stories, corners, downspouts, fascia condition, and whether the old system needs tearing off.

The worked example

Both rows below are this calculator's own built-in starting jobs — the brochure job the calculator itself labels "the $4.50/ft special," and the hardest job in its catalogue — priced at its own shipped shop rates: a $38/hr crew wage loaded at 32% burden to $50.16/hr, $95 travel and equipment, 16% overhead, a 32% target margin. The only thing that changes between them is the house.

QuestionThe brochure ranch — 140 ft, 5" aluminum, 4 outside miters, 2 downs includedWhere the special loses — 220 ft, 6" aluminum, 2-story, 2 inside miters, 4 downs, 40 ft fascia, tear-off
What the $4.50/ft special charges $630.00 — 140 ft × $4.50 $990.00 — 220 ft × $4.50, unchanged rate
Extras past the brochure ranch None — one story, no fascia, no tear-off Second story, 2 inside miters, 2 extra downspouts, 40 ft of fascia repair, tear-off of the old system
Total crew hours 8.10 h 32.26 h — almost 4× the crew time
Loaded labor cost ($50.16/hr) $406.30 $1,618.16
Material cost (trough, fittings, fascia, dump fee) $524.00 $2,262.60 — fascia and tear-off do not live in a per-foot rate
Total cost before any profit $1,189.34 $4,611.88
What the $4.50/ft special actually nets −$559.34 — covers loaded labor, not material or overhead −$3,621.88 — does not even cover loaded labor by $628.16
This calculator's price at a 32% target margin $1,749.03 $6,782.18 — $5,033.15 more than the brochure ranch, for the same $4.50/ft headline
Effective crew rate the $4.50/ft special actually pays $77.78/hr (8.10 billed hours) $30.69/hr — below the $50.16/hr loaded wage, at the identical advertised rate

The two places the flat rate goes quiet

1. Stories, corners, and fascia never separate from the trough

A flat per-foot rate answers "what do I charge per foot of gutter," not "how many stories, corners, extra drops, and feet of fascia this house needs." Both live inside the same $4.50 either way. The calculator splits them out — no extras on the brochure ranch, $2,262.60 of labor and material on the harder job — so a second story, inside miters, extra downspouts, and fascia repair are visible line items instead of one flat rate that happened to work out on a good day.

2. The same advertised rate does not scale with the house

This is the one that costs real money. The flat special charges $4.50 a foot whether the footage is on the brochure ranch or the hardest job in the catalogue, but the cost behind it is not the same — on this calculator's own defaults, the flat rate falls $559.34 short of cost on the ranch, and $3,621.88 short on the colonial, with the colonial's shortfall reaching all the way into the crew's own loaded wage. A shop quoting "the $4.50-a-foot special" on every call can sell every job on the sign and still lose money on the ones that turn out to need a second story and fascia repair, with nothing on the sign to say so.

When the flat special is still the better tool

For advertising, it plainly is. A yard sign or a web estimate cannot show a live calculator, and a homeowner calling for a price wants one number, not a form. The sensible arrangement is both: run the flat special to get the call, then run this calculator once you know the footage, profile, stories, miters, downspouts past the included allowance, fascia, and tear-off, to check whether that house's version of "the $4.50-a-foot job" still covers cost — and, on a house far enough from the brochure ranch, whether it needs a real bid instead.

Every figure on this page is this calculator's own worked example, computed from its own built-in starting jobs and shipped default shop rates, not a claim about any real shop's business or an industry benchmark. Your rates, wages, and overhead will produce different numbers — the point is which numbers to produce, not what they should come out to.

Common questions

Is a flat $4.50-a-foot special wrong?

No, and it should not go away. A yard sign or a web estimate needs one number, and "$4.50 a foot installed" is a fine headline rate. The point of this page is not that the flat rate is wrong — it is that the same per-foot number is charged whether the house is a square one-story ranch with two included downspouts or a two-story colonial with six-inch trough, extra drops, inside miters, fascia repair, and tear-off, and only a full bid separates the two.

Does the $4.50-a-foot special even cover the job it's named for?

On this calculator's own shipped defaults, barely, and not all the way. The preset this calculator itself labels "the $4.50/ft special" — a 140-foot one-story ranch in 5-inch aluminum, four outside miters, the first two downspouts included — costs $1,189.34 in total cost before any profit. The flat special prices that same job at $630.00: enough to clear the $406.30 loaded-labor cost, but $559.34 short of total cost once trough, fittings, travel, and overhead are counted, and $1,119.03 short of this calculator's own 32%-margin price.

How much worse does it get on a harder job?

A 220-foot two-story colonial in six-inch aluminum, two inside miters, four downspouts, 40 feet of fascia repair, and tear-off of the old system costs $4,611.88 in total cost on this calculator's own defaults. The same $4.50-a-foot rate prices that job at only $990.00 — $3,621.88 short of total cost, and $628.16 short of covering the crew's own loaded labor alone, before a single dollar of trough, fittings, fascia material, or overhead is counted.

Does the calculator replace the flat per-foot special?

No, and it is not trying to. The flat rate is what you advertise to get the call. This calculator is what you run once you know the footage, profile, stories, miters, downspouts past the included allowance, fascia, and tear-off, to check whether that house's version of "the $4.50-a-foot job" still covers cost — and, on a house far enough from the brochure ranch, whether it needs a real bid instead.

← Gutter Install Bid Calculator

This calculator vs. JobNimbus

Two different shapes: JobNimbus is an account-based CRM and job management platform for running an exterior contractor's whole lead-to-job pipeline. This page is a free, private worksheet for one question — what should this one gutter job cost, given its footage, profile, corners, and drops, before you send the bid.

What each tool is for

JobNimbus is a CRM and job management platform, founded in 2013 by Ben Hodson, Nick Wood, and Jason Wood, headquartered in Lehi, Utah. It is built for roofing, siding, gutter, solar, and other exterior contractors, covering lead and pipeline tracking, estimates and proposals, scheduling, job costing, and invoicing across a whole business, with a mobile app for crews in the field. It is an account-based platform: you sign up and use it as an ongoing service across a whole company, not a one-off calculator. JobNimbus's own pricing page is not reachable from this session to confirm today's exact plan names or dollar figures, so no price for it is invented here: only its well-documented identity and category — a CRM and job management platform serving exterior trades including gutter contractors, sold as a subscription account — are stated, and no dollar amount for JobNimbus appears on this page.

This calculator does none of what JobNimbus does. It does not track a lead, schedule a crew, or invoice a customer, and it stores no customer or job record on a server. It takes one gutter job's footage, profile (5-inch, 6-inch, or copper), stories, inside and outside miters, downspouts and downspout footage past the special's included allowance, fascia repair, tear-off, steep access, and hidden hangers, plus loaded installer wage, payroll burden, travel, overhead, and target margin, and turns that into the price, the price per foot of gutter, the effective hourly rate, and the walk-away price below which the job loses money — plus, if you already have a price on the table, a check of whether it clears that walk-away floor, and a single printable customer proposal for that one job. It runs free in any browser, keeps no account, and uploads nothing you type.

This page's own figures are a pricing model, not a lead record, a scheduled job, or a signed contract.

This tool needs no account and no sign-in: it is a static page, the arithmetic runs in your browser, and once it has loaded it keeps working with the connection off.

Should I use this calculator or JobNimbus?

They do different jobs, and a gutter company of any size will likely end up touching both eventually.
